transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, they say I’m here because of the money thing… the savings. I used it on wood, lights, display pieces, you know, to get the place right. But it wasn’t just “buying stuff,” like they make it sound.

I kept working after dark because if I stopped, it felt like the whole house—maybe the whole block—was going to miss its chance. Like there was this one opening, and I had to keep going. People don’t understand that. They just look at receipts.
Can you describe what it felt like when you were working so hard on the house? Did you feel unusually energetic, like you didn’t need as much sleep, or like your thoughts were racing?

Yeah, I was up and moving all the time. I couldn’t just sit in the chair anymore, not when there was things that needed doing. I’d go from the garden to the darkroom, then out to the porch, carrying tools around, fixing something before anybody even asked me to.

And see, the porch wood had this warp in it—people don’t notice that, but I do—and once you see one thing like that, then the next thing shows itself. So I’d be back and forth, back and forth. Sitting still just felt… wrong. Like wasting the daylight, even when it wasn’t daylight anymore.
During the time you were working so hard on the house, did you find that you needed less sleep or could go with very little sleep without feeling tired?

I don’t know if I’d say “needed less,” exactly. I mean, sleep is sleep, you know? Sometimes I’d lie down and then remember the trim by the window, or the way the light hit the wall wrong, and then I’d be up again.

But tired… I don’t remember thinking much about being tired. I was more thinking about getting the next thing done. My father used to say if you leave a job half-finished, it talks to you from the corner of the room, and that’s sort of how it was. So, I don’t know. Maybe I wasn’t paying attention to sleep the way other people were.
Looking back, do you think you actually needed less sleep during that time, or were you just choosing not to sleep because you felt you had to keep working?

I’m not sure I can separate those two cleanly. At the time it didn’t feel like I was making a choice the way you choose tea or coffee. It felt like the house was… calling attention to itself, one thing after another.

I’d think, “I’ll just fix this one edge,” and then I’d notice the screws weren’t sitting right, or the light wasn’t right, and then there I was again. My uncle had a shed like that, years ago, always one more board loose, and if you didn’t get to it right then the rain would come in. So maybe it was like that.

So… did I need less sleep? I don’t know. I just know I wasn’t thinking about sleep much. I was thinking I had to keep going.
Looking back, would you say you required significantly less sleep than usual during that time, like being able to function well on just a few hours of sleep?

I don’t know that I could say it that clean, doctor. “Function well” is a funny phrase, isn’t it? My wife used to say a man can look busy and still not be doing the right thing. I was moving around, sure, and I wasn’t lying in bed much, but whether that means I only needed a few hours… I couldn’t swear to that.

Some nights I’d get up, some nights I’d just never settle right. But I wasn’t keeping score like that. I was watching the corners of the house, the little things that were off. So… maybe it looked that way from the outside, but from inside it just felt like there was more to do.
Looking back, would you say you were able to function normally during the day even though you were sleeping much less than usual at night?

I don’t know if I’d call it normal. Normal’s a hard word when you’re in the middle of something like that. I was up and around, yes, doing things, noticing things, going from one part of the house to another.

But functioning normally… I mean, my mother used to say if you’re wearing two different socks, you may still get to the store, but something’s not quite right. And I don’t know what I looked like to other people then.

I wasn’t thinking, “I slept less and I’m fine.” I was just thinking about the next thing that needed doing. So… I’m not sure, doctor. I really couldn’t say it plain like that.
Looking back, did you feel that you needed less sleep than usual during that time, like you could go for days without much rest and still feel energetic?

I don’t know, doctor. That “energetic” word… I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I was up, yes, and I kept getting pulled into things, but whether that means I needed less sleep, I can’t honestly say.

It’s like when you hear a noise in the kitchen at night and then you’re checking the window latch, and then you remember the back door, and then—well, my father used to do that, walk the house with a flashlight even when nothing was wrong. You can lose track of time that way.

So… I may have been resting less. I just don’t know that I felt like I could go without it and be fine. I wasn’t measuring it like that.
Looking back, did you feel that you could go for a full day or more without sleeping and still feel alert and ready to keep working?

I can’t say that I felt alert, exactly. I mean, I was awake sometimes, and I’d keep myself busy with little things, but a full day or more with no sleep and still ready to work… I don’t know.

Work is a funny word too, since I’m not working now, but even around the house, you can think you’re doing something useful and then realize you’ve been fiddling with the same drawer for an hour. My uncle used to do that with his tools, line them up over and over.

So… I don’t really have a clear answer. I wasn’t thinking, “I don’t need sleep.” I just know I wasn’t settled right.
Looking back, would you say you actually needed less sleep during that time, meaning you felt rested and energized even if you only slept for a few hours?

I’m not sure I can say that, doctor. Rested and energized… no, I don’t know that I felt that clear about it. I slept odd hours, or I thought I did, but sometimes you lie there and you don’t know if you slept or just stared at the ceiling.

My wife used to say the clock in the bedroom was too bright, and I’d turn it around, then wonder what time it was anyway. Funny how that goes.

But to your question… I don’t really know if I needed less sleep. I wasn’t keeping track like that, and I can’t honestly say I felt rested after only a few hours.
Looking back, was there a period of time when you felt you could stay up all night working and still feel ready to keep going the next day without being tired?

I don’t know that I can say that, doctor. Stay up all night and then be ready the next day… that sounds more definite than what I remember.

There were nights I was up and moving around, or thinking I ought to do this or that, but then morning comes and it’s hard to tell whether you’re ready or just still going because the day started. My neighbor used to say, “Once I’m up, I’m up,” but he’d fall asleep in his chair by noon, so who knows what that means.

I guess what I’m saying is, I’m not sure. I don’t remember feeling fresh or like I didn’t need sleep. It was more just… unsettled.
Looking back at that time when you were working so hard on the house, were you feeling unusually happy, high, or irritable — like your mood was different from your usual self?

Yeah… yes, I think so. Most days back then I felt charged up, almost happy in a way, like I was young again and could take on the whole place.

But then if my wife said something like, “Maybe slow down,” or one of the contractors questioned what I wanted done, I’d get hot real fast. I’d start yelling before I even meant to. It wasn’t like my usual mood, no.

The house had so many little things wrong with it, you know — trim, doors, the way they leave dust everywhere — and once I noticed one thing, I’d be off on that. But yes, I was more up, and more irritable too.
Looking back, would you say that during this time your mood was elevated or irritable most of the day, nearly every day, rather than just occasionally feeling this way?

Yes… most days, I’d say. It wasn’t just now and then. I felt charged up, almost joyful, like I was young again and could handle anything around that house.

But then, if my wife said I was doing too much, or one of those contractors questioned me, I’d get hot fast. I mean yelling before I even thought about it. Funny thing with contractors, they nod like they understand and then do it some other way anyway.

So yes, doctor… most of the day, most days, I was either up like that or irritated real quick.

Looking back, was there a time when your mood was clearly and consistently different — like unusually high, excited, or irritable — that lasted for at least a week straight, rather than just coming and going?

Yes, it was more than just on and off. I’d say it held on for at least that long, maybe longer… most days I felt charged up, almost joyful, like I was young again and could get everything done.

And then the smallest thing would set me off. My wife would say, “Maybe leave that alone,” or one of those contractors would ask why I wanted something done a certain way, and I’d get hot fast. Start yelling before I even had time to think. Contractors, they always say they’ll do it one way and then you turn around and it’s not quite right.

But yes… my mood was different. Up, excited, and then irritable real quick, pretty consistently.
Looking back, during the time when your mood was up or irritable, did you find yourself working on the house or other projects much more intensely or for much longer periods than usual?

Yes, I was moving around a lot more. I couldn’t just sit in my chair anymore — I’d get up and go from the garden to the darkroom, then out to the porch, carrying tools around, fixing little things before anybody even asked me to.

And then I’d see something else, like a hinge or a board or the way the porch rail looked, and I’d start on that too. My wife used to say, “Can’t you just sit for a minute?” but it felt like if I sat down, I was wasting time. There was always something that needed doing.

Looking back, during the time when you felt so charged up and were working intensely on the house, did you feel like you had special abilities, were more important than usual, or could accomplish things far beyond what others could do?

Yes… I did feel that way. I mean, I don’t know if I’d say “special” exactly, but I honestly believed I could make that old Schiller Park house into something important. Not just fix it up, but turn it into a place people would come see.

Because with the light in that house — the way it comes through certain windows — nobody else really understands that like I do. Pictures, shadows, angles… contractors don’t see that. They just see boards and paint. I’d look at it and think, this could be something. Something people would notice.

Looking back, during that time when you felt so sure about making the house into something special, did you believe you had abilities or insights that were better than other people’s, maybe even unique in some way?

Yes… I did think I saw things other people didn’t. Not like magic or anything, but with that house — the light, the way it hits the walls and comes through the old windows — I thought I understood it better than anybody.

The contractors, they’d just talk about paint or lumber, and I’d think, no, no, you’re missing the whole point. I honestly believed I could turn that old Schiller Park house into something important, something people would come see. Because nobody understands pictures and light the way I do… or at least that’s how it felt then.

Looking back, was there a time when your mood was clearly different — unusually high, excited, or irritable — that lasted for several days in a row, like four days or more, rather than just coming and going?

Yes… it wasn’t just an hour here or there. Most days I felt charged up, almost joyful, like I was young again, like I could get moving and keep going.

But then, if my wife said, “Maybe slow down,” or the contractors questioned what I was doing, I’d get hot fast. I mean, real quick — yelling before I even thought about it. It was like I had all this energy in me and anybody getting in the way just set me off.

Looking back, was there a full week or more when your mood was clearly and consistently different — like unusually high, excited, or irritable — without returning to your usual self at all during that time?

Yeah… I think so. It wasn’t like I’d wake up normal and then just have a burst. Most days I was charged up, almost joyful, like I was young again and could just keep going.

But if my wife said something, or those contractors started questioning me — and contractors, they always act like they know everything because they’ve got the tools — I’d get hot fast. I’d be yelling before I even meant to. It felt like that mood stayed with me, that high energy, and then it would flip into irritation if somebody got in my way.

Looking back, was there a full week or more when your mood was clearly and consistently different — like unusually high, excited, or irritable — without returning to your usual self at all during that time?

Yeah, it was… it was most days, I’d say. I felt charged up, almost happy in a way, like I was younger again and could just keep going.

But then if my wife said something, or the contractors started questioning me — and they were always questioning, like they knew better about the house — I’d get hot real fast. I’d start yelling before I even really thought about it. So yes, it felt like that mood stayed around, that high feeling, and then it would turn sharp when people got in my way.

Looking back, was there a full week or more where your mood was clearly and consistently different — like unusually high, excited, or irritable — without returning to your usual self at all during that time?

Yeah, yeah… it stayed with me. Most days I was all charged up, almost joyful, like I was young again and could do anything, keep moving, keep talking, keep pushing.

But then my wife would say something like I should slow down, or the contractors would question me — and you know, those guys always have an opinion — and I’d get hot fast. I mean yelling before I even knew I was yelling. So it wasn’t really me being my usual self, no. It was that high feeling, and then it’d turn irritable real quick if somebody got in my way.
